items.title: L8: The Ministerial Code and the Civil Service Code
items.source: Ministerial Code, GOV.UK; Civil Service Code; Cabinet Manual
items.body: Ministers and civil servants are governed by different codes. The Ministerial Code, issued by the Prime Minister, sets out the standards of conduct expected of ministers. It includes the principle that ministers have a duty to Parliament to account, and to be as open as possible; that it is of paramount importance that ministers give accurate and truthful information to Parliament, correcting any inadvertent error at the earliest opportunity; and that ministers must not knowingly mislead Parliament. It also covers handling of private interests, use of government resources, and the relationship with civil servants. The Prime Minister is the ultimate judge of the standards of behaviour expected of a minister and of the appropriate consequences of a breach. The Prime Minister can ask the Independent Adviser on Ministers' Interests to investigate, and the Adviser advises the Prime Minister rather than deciding the outcome. The Civil Service Code, by contrast, sets out the values and standards expected of civil servants: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. It is part of every civil servant's terms and conditions and is given statutory force by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010. The two codes interact. The Ministerial Code says ministers should uphold the political impartiality of the Civil Service and not ask civil servants to act in ways that conflict with the Civil Service Code. A civil servant who is asked to do something inconsistent with the Civil Service Code should raise it through the Code's routes. The Civil Service Commission can hear complaints that the Civil Service Code has been breached. No equivalent independent route exists for enforcing the Ministerial Code, which is why the Prime Minister's judgement is decisive.

questions.prompt: Who has the final say on whether a minister has breached the Ministerial Code and what follows?

options.text: The Prime Minister, who may take advice from the Independent Adviser
The Independent Adviser on Ministers' Interests, whose findings are binding on the minister
The Cabinet Secretary, as head of the Civil Service and keeper of the Code
The Civil Service Commission, once officials have complained to it

questions.hint: The Adviser investigates and advises; the Prime Minister decides.

questions.prompt: A minister asks officials to prepare material attacking the opposition for a party rally. Which code is most directly engaged?

options.text: Only the Ministerial Code, because it concerns the minister's own behaviour
Both: it conflicts with the Civil Service Code and with the Ministerial Code's duty to uphold impartiality
Only the Civil Service Code, because ministers cannot be bound by any written rules
Neither, because the request concerns a party event and not the department's business

questions.hint: Each code covers a side of the same problem.

questions.prompt: What does the Ministerial Code require when a minister realises they gave Parliament inaccurate information by mistake?

options.text: Wait until the end of the parliamentary session before raising it, so it can be dealt with in one go
Leave it unless an opposition MP notices the error and complains
Correct the record at the earliest opportunity
Ask officials to quietly update the department's website without telling Parliament

questions.hint: Accuracy is paramount, and errors are corrected promptly.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts the two codes?

options.text: Both codes are enforced by the Civil Service Commission in the same way
Both were set by Parliament in the same Act and have the same enforcement
The Ministerial Code applies to civil servants in private offices as well as to ministers
The Civil Service Code has statutory force and an independent complaint route; the Ministerial Code does not

questions.prompt: An official in a private office believes a minister's instruction conflicts with the Civil Service Code. What is the first appropriate step?

options.text: Raise it with a line manager or the nominated officer, following the Code's routes
Tell the Independent Adviser on Ministers' Interests directly, as the minister's conduct is involved
Refuse to work for that minister and ask to be moved at once
Report it to the Speaker of the House of Commons, who protects officials

questions.hint: The Civil Service Code's own routes come first.

questions.prompt: Which duty is NOT in the Ministerial Code but is in the Civil Service Code?

options.text: The duty to account to Parliament for the work of a department
The duty not to knowingly mislead Parliament
The expectation that holders of office behave with integrity
The value of impartiality as applied to serving any government

questions.hint: The impartiality value belongs to the Civil Service Code.

questions.prompt: Why do many observers say the Ministerial Code's enforcement is weaker than the Civil Service Code's?

options.text: Because ministers are exempt from the Code when they act in the public interest
It depends on the Prime Minister's judgement rather than an independent body with powers
Because the Code is not written down and depends on unwritten practice
Because the Code applies only to former ministers after they leave office

questions.hint: The Prime Minister is the arbiter.

questions.prompt: The Civil Service Code is part of civil servants' terms and conditions. What does that mean in practice?

options.text: Civil servants can ignore it if their minister disagrees with a provision
Only a court can enforce it, never the employer
Breaches can be handled through the department's conduct and disciplinary processes
It also binds ministers in the same way as it binds their officials

questions.hint: The Code is a condition of employment.

items.title: L8: Collective responsibility and cabinet committees
items.body: Collective responsibility means that, once the government has reached a decision, all ministers are expected to support it in public, and that discussions leading to it remain confidential. The reason is that ministers can disagree frankly inside government, and then present a united position. The Cabinet is the final decision-making body, but most business is settled in Cabinet committees, which are smaller groups of ministers chaired by a senior minister, often the Prime Minister or another Cabinet member. Committees take decisions that bind the whole government unless the matter is referred upwards. The Cabinet Office runs the secretariat, circulates papers, records the conclusions and chases action. A department that wishes to propose a major policy normally writes a paper for the relevant committee, after consulting other departments with an interest. Treasury views on spending are essential. A key rule of procedure is that issues should be resolved at the lowest level, so that only unresolved disagreements go to committee, and only the most contentious or important to the full Cabinet. A write-round is a quicker way of getting agreement when a meeting is unnecessary: the lead minister writes to colleagues with a proposal and a deadline, and silence by the deadline is taken as agreement. Officials need to advise their minister on who must be consulted and on the handling of the paper. Cabinet papers and discussions are protected by the confidentiality convention, and the Cabinet Secretary can advise on the handling of past papers. Ministers who find they cannot support a collective decision traditionally resign. Officials must keep the record of what was decided so that departments know what is required of them.

questions.prompt: A minister disagrees privately with a Cabinet decision but must defend it in public. Which principle does this show?

options.text: Individual ministerial responsibility
Political impartiality
Accounting officer responsibility
Collective responsibility

questions.hint: Collective responsibility binds ministers to the decision.

questions.prompt: A department wants approval for a policy that has implications for two other departments. What is the usual first practical step?

options.text: Send it straight to the full Cabinet, which will resolve the differences itself
Announce the policy and amend it after the other departments react
Consult the departments concerned and seek agreement or resolve differences before it goes to committee
Ask the Treasury to decide the matter for all the departments concerned

questions.hint: Issues are resolved at the lowest level first.

questions.prompt: What is a write-round used for in Cabinet business?

options.text: A press briefing for journalists before a Cabinet meeting
A way of seeking agreement by letter, where silence by the deadline counts as agreement
A draft of a Bill sent to Parliamentary Counsel for drafting
A review of last year's decisions to see whether they were delivered

questions.prompt: Which body typically runs the Cabinet and Cabinet committee secretariat?

options.text: The Cabinet Office
The Treasury, which also controls the spending of every Cabinet committee
The Home Office, which hosts the committee meetings
The Government Legal Department, which advises each committee

questions.hint: The Cabinet Office records and circulates.

questions.prompt: Why must Cabinet discussions remain confidential?

options.text: So ministers can disagree frankly in private and then present a united position
Because the Official Secrets Act covers every Cabinet paper automatically
Because Parliament is forbidden by law from seeing any Cabinet discussion
Because the Speaker has ruled that Cabinet records may never be published

questions.prompt: Which description fits what a Cabinet committee decision does?

options.text: It is advice that departments may follow or ignore as they choose
It is a draft that Parliament will normally amend before it applies
It binds the whole government unless referred up
It applies only to the minister who happens to chair the committee

questions.prompt: A minister cannot bring themselves to support a collective decision. What is the traditional response?

options.text: Stay in government and criticise the decision openly
Resign from the government
Ask civil servants to change the decision before it is announced
Attend Cabinet but refuse to vote, while staying in post

questions.prompt: A policy official forgets to include the Treasury in a cross-government paper that has spending implications. Why is this a serious omission?

options.text: The Treasury would automatically cancel the policy as soon as it found out
The Treasury would take over writing the paper for all departments
The Cabinet would be unable to read a paper without a Treasury cover sheet
Treasury agreement is needed for spending, so the paper could be returned and the minister embarrassed

items.title: L8: Business cases and spending controls
items.source: HM Treasury, The Green Book and Managing Public Money; Infrastructure and Projects Authority guidance
items.body: Public money is controlled by Parliament and managed by the Treasury. Departments cannot spend as they please. Each year Parliament approves departmental spending through the Estimates process, and the Treasury sets spending limits through Spending Reviews. Within those limits, departments have delegated authority to spend, but only up to set levels. Larger or more unusual proposals need approval from the Treasury, and the largest or riskiest are subject to spending controls. Proposals are usually put forward in a business case. Following the Green Book, the Five Case Model has five parts: the strategic case, which explains why the change is needed and how it fits policy; the economic case, which compares options by their costs and benefits to society; the commercial case, which sets out how the goods and services will be procured; the financial case, which shows affordability and funding; and the management case, which explains how the project will be delivered, with governance, risks and benefits tracking. A business case is developed in stages: a strategic outline case, an outline business case and a full business case, with approval at each stage. Major projects are monitored by the Infrastructure and Projects Authority, which provides assurance reviews and rates the likelihood of successful delivery. Gateway reviews at key points can recommend changes. Accounting officers must be satisfied that a proposal meets the four standards of regularity, propriety, value for money and feasibility. Officials who spend beyond their authority risk creating irregular expenditure that must be reported and may be qualified in the accounts.

questions.prompt: Which case in the Five Case Model sets out whether the proposal is affordable and how it will be funded?

options.text: The financial case
The strategic case, which sets out why the change is needed
The management case, which sets out how it will be delivered
The economic case, which compares options by costs and benefits

questions.prompt: A business case shows excellent benefits but has no plan for who would manage delivery or track risks. Which part is weak?

options.text: The commercial case
The strategic case
The economic case
The management case

questions.hint: The management case covers delivery arrangements.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the economic case?

options.text: To set out how the goods or services will be bought from suppliers
To compare options by their costs and benefits to society
To prove that the budget has been agreed by the Treasury
To list the members of the project team and their roles

questions.prompt: Why are business cases often developed in stages?

options.text: Because the Treasury will read only short documents of a few pages
Because each stage must be written by a different team of officials
So that approval can be given and tested at each stage before more money is committed
Because Parliament requires three separate drafts before it votes the money

questions.prompt: Who sets the spending limits for each department over the Spending Review period?

options.text: The Cabinet Office, which controls the Spending Review process
The Treasury
The National Audit Office, which audits whether limits are respected
The Speaker, who approves departmental spending in the Commons

questions.prompt: What does the Infrastructure and Projects Authority do?

options.text: Writes the Estimates that Parliament votes on each year
Audits departmental accounts for Parliament after the year ends
Appoints the project director in every department with a major project
Provides assurance and reviews of major government projects

questions.hint: It supports delivery of major projects.

questions.prompt: A manager approves a purchase over their delegated limit. What risk does this create?

options.text: Irregular expenditure that may need to be reported and explained
Nothing, if the purchase turns out to be good value for money
A criminal charge against the manager, automatically
A requirement for the manager to repay the supplier personally

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the purpose of Estimates?

options.text: They estimate how much tax the Treasury expects to raise in a year
They record the previous year's spending in the published accounts
They seek Parliament's authority for departments to spend
They set pay scales for civil service grades across departments

items.title: L8: Departmental boards and governance
items.source: Cabinet Office, Corporate governance in central government departments: code of good practice
items.body: Every main government department has a board. The departmental board is chaired by the Secretary of State or a senior minister and includes ministers, senior civil servants and independent non-executive directors from outside government. The board provides collective leadership: it sets the strategy, monitors performance, and challenges how risks are managed. The permanent secretary is the principal accounting officer and is accountable for the department's performance, but the board does not replace ministerial accountability or the permanent secretary's personal responsibility. Non-executive board members are appointed to bring external experience and constructive challenge; they are not civil servants and have no power to direct officials. A lead non-executive member often chairs the audit and risk assurance committee, which reviews the department's internal controls, risk management and the accounts. The committee works with internal audit, such as the Government Internal Audit Agency, and with the National Audit Office, which audits the accounts for Parliament. Internal audit gives independent assurance to the accounting officer, and the National Audit Office reports to Parliament. A well-run department follows the three lines of defence: day-to-day management controls, oversight functions such as finance and risk teams, and independent assurance from internal and external audit. Boards also look at people issues, including workforce capability and diversity. Directors may report to the board on the delivery of key programmes. The board's role is advisory and supportive but must be clear about its decisions and record them. A department's annual report and accounts include a governance statement, signed by the accounting officer, which describes how risks and controls are managed and any significant issues.

questions.prompt: Who signs the governance statement in the annual report and accounts?

options.text: The accounting officer
The lead non-executive board member, who chairs the audit committee
The Secretary of State, as the minister in charge
The Comptroller and Auditor General, who audits the accounts

questions.hint: The accounting officer is responsible for it.

questions.prompt: What is the main contribution of non-executive board members?

options.text: Directing officials on policy in place of ministers
Setting the minister's priorities for the department
Approving every spending decision taken inside the department
External experience and constructive challenge

questions.prompt: Which body gives independent assurance directly to the accounting officer?

options.text: The National Audit Office, which reports to Parliament
Internal audit
The Public Accounts Committee, which questions officials in public
The Information Commissioner, who regulates data handling

questions.hint: Internal audit supports the accounting officer; the NAO reports to Parliament.

questions.prompt: Which describes the 'three lines of defence'?

options.text: Ministers, officials and the public, each checking the other
Parliament, the courts and the press, each scrutinising the department
Management controls, oversight functions and independent assurance
Budgets, targets and rewards, applied to each programme in turn

questions.prompt: A board member suggests the board should replace the permanent secretary as the person accountable to Parliament for the spending. What is wrong with this?

options.text: Board members are not allowed to speak at meetings, so the idea could not work
Accounting officer responsibility is personal and cannot be handed to a board
The Treasury has banned departmental boards from taking any decisions
Boards cannot see financial data, so they could not carry the responsibility

questions.prompt: What does the audit and risk assurance committee review?

options.text: Ministers' diaries and their travel arrangements
Recruitment panels and the marking of applications
Parliamentary questions and the answers drafted for them
Internal controls, risk management and the accounts

questions.prompt: Who audits a department's accounts for Parliament?

options.text: The National Audit Office
The Government Internal Audit Agency
The Treasury, through its spending teams
The Cabinet Office, through its propriety team

questions.prompt: The board challenges a programme because delivery is behind schedule. Which role is it playing?

options.text: Replacing the programme director with an external appointment
Instructing contractors directly about how to do their work
Monitoring performance and challenging risk management
Approving the department's Estimates for the coming year

items.title: L8: Risk management and the Orange Book
items.source: HM Treasury, The Orange Book: Management of Risk – Principles and Concepts
items.body: The Orange Book is the Treasury's guidance on risk management in government. It says risk management should be part of how an organisation is led and managed and should help it meet its objectives, not be a separate paperwork exercise. A risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives, usually described by its likelihood and impact. Organisations keep a risk register that lists risks, their owners, their rating, and the controls and actions in place. Risks are rated before controls (inherent risk) and after controls (residual risk). The organisation decides its risk appetite, meaning how much risk it is willing to take to achieve objectives, which varies by area; for example, a department may have a low appetite for risk in handling personal data but a higher appetite for trying new ways of delivering services. Typical responses to a risk are to tolerate it, treat it by adding controls, transfer it, for example through insurance or contract terms, or terminate the activity. Each risk should have a named owner who is responsible for managing it and escalating when it exceeds tolerance. Risks are escalated up through the organisation to the board when they are significant. A good risk culture encourages staff to speak up about problems early without blame. The risk register is a living document reviewed regularly. A risk that has happened becomes an issue, which is managed differently. Programmes also keep their own risk registers and feed significant risks to the department's. Good risk management also looks at emerging risks, such as new technology or changes in the supply chain.

questions.prompt: A department has a low appetite for risk in protecting personal data but a higher appetite for experiments in service design. What does this show?

options.text: The department has not decided on a risk strategy
Risk appetite can differ between areas of activity
Risk appetite must be the same for every activity in a department
The Treasury sets risk appetite for each activity in every department

questions.prompt: What is meant by residual risk in a risk register?

options.text: The level of risk that existed before any action was taken
A risk that has already happened and is now being managed
The level of risk that remains after controls have been applied
A risk that cannot be given a rating because it is too uncertain

questions.prompt: A risk becomes real and starts causing delays. How is it now classed?

options.text: As an inherent risk
As a tolerated risk
As an opportunity
As an issue, which is managed differently

questions.hint: A risk that has happened becomes an issue.

questions.prompt: Which response is 'transferring' a risk?

options.text: Using insurance or contract terms to move the impact to another party
Adding more checks to a process to reduce the likelihood
Stopping the activity entirely so the risk no longer arises
Accepting the risk and monitoring it without further action

questions.prompt: Why should each risk have a named owner?

options.text: So that someone can be blamed if the risk happens
So that the Treasury can audit each risk individually
So that someone is responsible for managing it and escalating if needed
So that Parliament can question the owner about it

questions.prompt: Which culture best supports effective risk management?

options.text: Staff avoid reporting uncertain risks until they are sure they are real
Staff speak up about problems early without blame
Only senior staff are allowed to discuss risks with the board
Risks are reviewed once a year, which keeps the process light

questions.prompt: What does the risk register provide?

options.text: A living record of risks, owners, ratings, controls and actions
A list of the staff who have made mistakes in the past year
The budget for the department for the coming year
A record of parliamentary questions and the risks they raise

questions.prompt: When should a programme risk be escalated to the department's board?

options.text: Whenever the programme starts, so the board sees every risk
Only once it has caused real harm to the programme
Never, since boards deal with finance and not with programme risk
When it is significant or exceeds the programme's tolerance

items.title: L8: Environmental information and the public interest test
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000; Environmental Information Regulations 2004; ICO guidance
items.body: Freedom of Information requests are not the only way people can ask for government information. The Environmental Information Regulations 2004 (EIR) give a separate right of access to environmental information, which covers things like air and water quality, land use, waste, and the policies and decisions that affect the environment. If a request is for environmental information, it must be handled under the EIR rather than the Freedom of Information Act, even if the requester refers to FOI. Requests under EIR can be made verbally or in writing, with a response normally due within 20 working days. Under both regimes, public authorities should consider the public interest when applying qualified exemptions or exceptions. For FOI, the public interest test asks whether the public interest in maintaining the exemption outweighs the public interest in disclosure. The test looks at the specific harm from disclosure and the specific benefit, for example in accountability, transparency and public debate. The ICO has said that safe space arguments can be relevant to policy formulation, which means that officials need space to consider options freely, but that the need for it reduces once the decision has been made. Under EIR, exceptions are all subject to the public interest test and there is a presumption in favour of disclosure. Authorities must also publish certain information proactively through a publication scheme. If an authority withholds information, it must explain which exemption applies and why, and tell the requester how to complain. Some information, such as the requester's own personal data, is dealt with under data protection law instead. When the requester is not satisfied, they can ask for an internal review, then complain to the ICO, which can issue a decision notice that is legally binding, and appeal to the First-tier Tribunal.

questions.prompt: A request asks for data on local air quality and cites the Freedom of Information Act. Which regime applies?

options.text: The Freedom of Information Act, because the requester cited it
The Data Protection Act, because air quality data is collected from people
The Environmental Information Regulations, because it is environmental information
The Official Secrets Act, because the data is held by government

questions.hint: The type of information decides the regime.

questions.prompt: How do the rules on making a request differ for environmental information?

options.text: Verbal requests are accepted under EIR, though FOI requires writing
EIR requests must be made on a form supplied by the authority
EIR requests must be made by letter, because they are formal legal requests
EIR requests can be made only through the authority's website

questions.hint: EIR is more flexible than FOI on this.

questions.prompt: The public interest test, when applied to a qualified exemption, asks which question?

options.text: Whether the minister approves disclosure of the information
Whether the requester is a journalist or a private individual
Whether the information is old enough to have lost its sensitivity
Whether the public interest in withholding outweighs the public interest in disclosure

questions.prompt: How does the safe space argument change over time for policy advice?

options.text: It carries more weight after the decision, since the policy is then in place
It carries less weight once the decision has been taken
It never applies, since the Act contains no such principle
It always overrides disclosure for any policy advice

questions.hint: Safe space matters while policy is live.

questions.prompt: A requester wants a copy of their own medical record held by a department. How should this be handled?

options.text: As an FOI request only, with the same exemptions for personal information
As an EIR request, since medical information concerns health
As a complaint about the department's handling of data
As a subject access request under data protection law

questions.hint: Own personal data is outside FOI.

questions.prompt: What can the ICO do if it finds that an authority wrongly withheld information?

options.text: Fine the minister who approved the refusal
Replace the authority's FOI officer with a nominee of its own
Issue a decision notice requiring disclosure
Take over the authority's handling of requests for a year

questions.prompt: Which of these is an authority obliged to do under the Act, even without a request?

options.text: Publish all internal emails, to show how decisions are made
Maintain a publication scheme
Publish the salaries of staff below grade 7 in every case
Publish ministers' diaries each month, whether or not asked

questions.prompt: After a final ICO decision, a dissatisfied party can appeal to which body?

options.text: The First-tier Tribunal
The Civil Service Commission
The Cabinet Office
The House of Lords

items.title: L8: Devolution in more depth
items.source: Scotland Act 1998; Government of Wales Act 2006; Northern Ireland Act 1998; Cabinet Office, Devolution guidance for civil servants
items.body: Devolution settlements differ between Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and they have evolved through later Acts. The Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd have wide powers over devolved matters, while Northern Ireland has its own arrangements, with an Executive that shares power between parties. The UK Parliament remains sovereign and could legislate on devolved matters. The Sewel convention, however, says that the UK Parliament will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the consent of the devolved legislature, which is given by a legislative consent motion. Civil servants in UK departments working on legislation that touches devolved areas must consult their counterparts and seek that consent. Concordats and, more recently, intergovernmental relations structures provide the means for UK and devolved governments to work together, with ministerial councils, and ways of resolving disputes. Officials from different governments share data and engage informally, but each serves its own ministers. Scottish and Welsh Government civil servants work for devolved ministers and are accountable through them to their parliaments, even though they are part of the Home Civil Service and bound by the Civil Service Code. Funding for devolved governments comes mainly through a block grant from the UK Treasury, adjusted using the Barnett formula when UK spending on comparable services changes in England. Devolved governments have some tax and borrowing powers. In practice, many policy areas require cooperation, for example public health and food standards, and common frameworks have been agreed to manage them. When UK government policy affects devolved areas, good practice is early engagement, particularly before announcements.

questions.prompt: What does the Sewel convention say?

options.text: The UK Parliament may not legislate on devolved matters under any circumstances
Devolved legislatures must agree to all UK Bills before they can become Acts
The UK Parliament will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the devolved legislature's consent
Devolved governments decide UK foreign policy in the areas that affect them

questions.hint: It is a convention, not a legal bar.

questions.prompt: How is the legislative consent normally given?

options.text: By a legislative consent motion in the devolved legislature
By a letter from the First Minister alone, once they have considered the Bill
By the UK Prime Minister, after talks with devolved ministers
By the Supreme Court, when it rules that the Bill is acceptable

questions.hint: A motion in the devolved parliament.

questions.prompt: A civil servant in the Scottish Government is bound by which code?

options.text: A separate Scottish code of conduct only, drawn up by the Scottish Parliament
The Ministerial Code, because they serve ministers
The Code of Conduct for Special Advisers, because they serve politicians
The Civil Service Code, while serving Scottish ministers

questions.hint: They are in the Home Civil Service.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the Barnett formula?

options.text: It sets the rates of income tax paid in Scotland
It adjusts the block grant when UK spending on comparable services in England changes
It decides which matters are devolved and which are reserved
It allocates seats in the Senedd between the parties

questions.prompt: A UK department plans an announcement that affects health policy in Wales. What is good practice?

options.text: Announce first and brief the Welsh Government afterwards to keep the news clean
Wait for the Welsh Government to raise concerns before engaging
Engage the Welsh Government early, before the announcement
Ask Welsh civil servants to approve the announcement before it is made

questions.prompt: Why are common frameworks used?

options.text: To remove devolved powers over the areas where rules interact
To merge the UK and devolved civil services in those areas
To fix the number of members of each devolved parliament
To manage cooperation in policy areas where devolved and UK rules interact

questions.prompt: An official in a UK department works with a counterpart in the Scottish Government. Whom does each serve?

options.text: Both serve the UK Prime Minister in a joint capacity
Each serves their own ministers
Both serve the Scottish First Minister when working together
Both serve the Cabinet Secretary, who coordinates joint working

questions.prompt: Which statement about the UK Parliament's power is correct?

options.text: It remains sovereign and could legislate on devolved matters
It has given up the power permanently, so it cannot now legislate
It may legislate only for England, in areas that are devolved elsewhere
It needs the Supreme Court's permission before legislating on devolved matters

items.title: L8: Local government and delivery chains
items.source: Local Government Act 1972 and 2000; Cabinet Office, delivery chain guidance; Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
items.body: Many public services are delivered not by Whitehall but by councils and other local bodies. Local authorities are elected, have their own legal powers, and are accountable to local voters as well as being subject to national legislation. A central department cannot simply order a council to do something unless the law gives the power. Departments instead use legislation, funding, guidance, inspection and performance frameworks to influence what councils do. Council funding comes from council tax, business rates, fees and government grants, and councils have a legal duty to balance their budgets. Many functions are statutory duties, for example adult social care, children's services, waste collection and planning. Others are discretionary. When government wants a change in a service run by councils, it faces a delivery chain: a policy is set in a department, passed through guidance and funding to councils, who deliver it through teams and often contractors. Each link affects what the public experiences. Delay and loss of focus can happen along the chain, which is why departments try to understand delivery early and test policies with local partners. Accountability is shared: ministers are accountable for national policy and the framework, but a council's elected members and its chief executive are accountable for local decisions. If a council is failing, the government has powers to intervene, such as appointing commissioners, but uses them rarely and with caution. For the public, complaints about local services start with the council, then the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman. Departments need to avoid taking credit or blame for what is local. Civil servants should be clear about what is central and what is local when advising callers or ministers.

questions.prompt: A minister wants a council to change how it collects waste. What can the department rely on?

options.text: A simple written instruction from the minister, which councils must follow
A request to the Prime Minister to overrule the council
Legislation, funding, guidance and oversight, unless the law gives it power to direct
The Civil Service Code, which binds councils as well as officials

questions.hint: Councils have their own legal powers.

questions.prompt: Which body handles complaints about local councils once the council's own process is exhausted?

options.text: The Parliamentary Ombudsman, who covers all public services
The Civil Service Commission, which hears complaints about public bodies
The Cabinet Office, which handles complaints about local services
The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for a council's local decisions?

options.text: The relevant Secretary of State, who answers for all council decisions
Its elected members and chief executive
The Prime Minister, as head of government
The head of the Civil Service, who oversees councils

questions.prompt: A new national policy is slowed by guidance that reaches councils late. What is this an example of?

options.text: A weakness in the delivery chain
A breach of the Sewel convention
A failure of collective responsibility
A misuse of the Estimates procedure

questions.hint: Delays along the chain affect results.

questions.prompt: Why do departments test policies with local partners before launch?

options.text: To avoid needing legislation for the policy
To pass accountability for the policy to councils
To reduce the funding that the policy would otherwise need
To understand delivery problems early

questions.prompt: Which of these is a statutory duty for many councils?

options.text: Running the national railways
Issuing passports
Adult social care
Defence procurement

questions.prompt: In very serious cases of failure, what can central government do?

options.text: Intervene, for example by appointing commissioners
Dismiss the council's staff directly and appoint replacements
Take over council tax collection from the next financial year
Close the council and merge it with its neighbour

questions.hint: Powers exist but are used rarely.

questions.prompt: A caller asks you to fix a pothole on their road. What should you do?

options.text: Log it with the department so it can be passed to the minister
Explain that the local council is responsible and point to how to report it
Tell them to write to the Prime Minister
Say that the Treasury handles road repairs

questions.hint: Be clear about central versus local.

items.title: L8: Protected disclosures in more detail
items.source: Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (Employment Rights Act 1996, Part IVA); Civil Service Code
items.body: The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 inserted provisions into the Employment Rights Act 1996 that protect workers who blow the whistle. To qualify for protection, a disclosure must be a qualifying disclosure: the worker must reasonably believe that it is made in the public interest and that it tends to show one of a list of matters, for example a criminal offence, a failure to comply with a legal obligation, a miscarriage of justice, a danger to health and safety, damage to the environment, or deliberate concealment of any of these. The disclosure must be made in the right way. The most protected route is to the employer or a person the employer has told staff to report to. Disclosures to a prescribed person, such as a regulator named in regulations, are also protected if the worker reasonably believes the information is substantially true and falls within that regulator's remit. Disclosures to the wider public, for instance the media, are protected only in narrower circumstances, such as where the worker reasonably believes that they would suffer a detriment if they raised the matter internally, or that evidence would be concealed, or if the concern has already been raised and nothing was done, and it must be reasonable to disclose publicly. Workers are protected from dismissal and from other detriment because they made the disclosure. A worker does not need to be right, but they must have a reasonable belief. Those who disclose classified material face additional restrictions, because the Official Secrets Act 1989 is not subject to the same public interest defence. Civil servants should therefore think about security and legal advice before disclosing outside the usual channels. The Civil Service Code encourages internal reporting first, and departments are expected to deal with concerns seriously and protect staff from retaliation.

questions.prompt: Which belief must a worker hold for a disclosure to qualify for protection?

options.text: That it is proven and the employer has had time to fix it
That it is in the public interest and tends to show a listed type of wrongdoing
That the employer will fix it once told
That it has already been reported in the press

questions.prompt: A worker raises a concern with a regulator named in the regulations, about a matter in the regulator's remit. What is the position?

options.text: It can be a protected disclosure if the worker reasonably believes the information is substantially true
It is never protected, because only disclosures to the employer count
It is protected only if the employer has approved the disclosure
It is protected only if the information has already been published

questions.hint: Prescribed persons are a protected route.

questions.prompt: Which is a stricter route for protection?

options.text: A disclosure to the employer
A disclosure to the whistleblowing officer
A disclosure to the media
A disclosure to a prescribed regulator

questions.prompt: A civil servant reasonably believes there is a danger to public health but turns out to be mistaken. Does protection still apply?

options.text: Protection is lost automatically if the concern turns out to be wrong
Protection applies only to workers at a senior grade, whatever the result
Protection applies only if the worker also told the press
It can, because the worker needs only a reasonable belief, not to be proven right

questions.prompt: What does protection from detriment cover?

options.text: Dismissal and other unfair treatment because of the disclosure
Only dismissal, and not other kinds of treatment
Only pay cuts that follow a disclosure
Only demotion within the same department

questions.prompt: Why should a civil servant be careful before disclosing classified information externally?

options.text: Because classified information is always inaccurate and so cannot be disclosed
The Official Secrets Act 1989 has no equivalent public interest defence
Because the Civil Service Code forbids all reporting of concerns
Because the Commission fines anyone disclosing classified information

questions.prompt: According to the Civil Service Code, where should concerns generally go first?

options.text: To the press, so that the public can judge
To the local MP, who can raise it in Parliament
Through internal routes, such as the line manager or a nominated officer
To a prescribed regulator, before telling the employer

questions.prompt: A worker raises a concern, then is moved to a less favourable role. What might this be?

options.text: A normal reorganisation, if it follows the usual process
An approved performance process that had already been planned
A requirement of the Code, which says disclosers must move
A detriment that may be unlawful if connected to the disclosure

items.title: L8: Leaving government: business appointment rules
items.source: Business Appointment Rules for Crown servants; Advisory Committee on Business Appointments (ACOBA)
items.body: When civil servants leave to take jobs outside government, they could use inside knowledge or contacts unfairly, or could be suspected of having been influenced while in post by the prospect of future work. To manage this, the Business Appointment Rules require former Crown servants to seek approval before taking up some new jobs. Departments apply the rules to staff at senior levels and to staff in roles that give particular access to sensitive information or commercial influence. Applications are considered by the department, which decides whether to approve and under what conditions. For the most senior civil servants and special advisers, applications also go to the Advisory Committee on Business Appointments, known as ACOBA, which is an independent body that gives advice. ACOBA considers whether the new role could give unfair advantage or lead to a perception that the former official acted improperly. Conditions can include a waiting period, a ban on lobbying government for a set time, a ban on using privileged information, and a restriction on working on particular contracts. Officials must not start the new role until permission has been given. The rules also apply to people who leave briefly or who take unpaid roles. Before leaving, staff are expected to declare any approach from a potential employer and to step back from relevant decisions. Failing to follow the rules is a breach of the Code and may bring consequences, such as disciplinary action, a reference to the Cabinet Office, or in extreme cases loss of pension rights. The aim is to protect public confidence that decisions are taken in the public interest, not for future private benefit. Contact with former colleagues is acceptable if it follows the rules but staff should avoid giving privileged treatment to former colleagues.

questions.prompt: A senior official has been offered a job with a company that bids for work with their department. What should they do first?

options.text: Accept it and tell their line manager later when the offer is confirmed
Wait until the contract has been awarded to say anything
Say nothing until they have left the Civil Service
Declare the approach, step back from relevant decisions and apply under the rules

questions.prompt: What is ACOBA's role in the business appointment rules?

options.text: An independent body that gives advice on applications from the most senior leavers
It approves every job taken by any civil servant who leaves
It runs the department's recruitment campaigns
It audits business expenses claimed by departments

questions.prompt: Which condition is commonly applied to a new role?

options.text: A requirement to stay in the Civil Service for at least five years
A period during which the former official must not lobby government
A permanent bar on working in the private sector
A requirement to report weekly to the former minister

questions.prompt: Why do the business appointment rules exist at all?

options.text: To prevent civil servants from ever taking higher paid jobs outside
To keep experienced staff inside the Civil Service
To protect confidence that decisions are taken in the public interest
To stop former officials working for any private company

questions.prompt: A former official joins a supplier and starts calling former colleagues to lobby for an advantage. How should serving staff respond?

options.text: Provide extra information, because they are friends and the rules no longer apply
Ignore the rules because the person has left government
Ask them for a job at their new company
Treat the contact in line with the rules and avoid giving privileged treatment

questions.prompt: A senior official's permission is still pending. May they start the new job early?

options.text: They should wait, because permission must be obtained before starting
They may start if the new role is unpaid
They may start if the appointment is short term
They may start if their line manager agrees informally

questions.prompt: What might follow a breach of the business appointment rules?

options.text: Nothing further, because the person has already left the Civil Service
A fine imposed under the Official Secrets Act 1989
Disciplinary action or a referral, and in extreme cases loss of pension rights
A criminal prosecution under the Bribery Act in every case

questions.prompt: The rules apply to which of these?

options.text: Only the Cabinet Secretary, as the most senior official
Senior staff and others in roles with sensitive access or commercial influence
Only people who leave in disgrace
Only people who retire on a full pension

items.title: L8: How the Civil Service Commission handles complaints
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Guidance on complaints and Code investigations; Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010
items.body: The Civil Service Commission is an independent body set up in law by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010. It has two main jobs: regulating recruitment to the Civil Service, and hearing appeals from civil servants who think they have been asked to act in a way that conflicts with the Civil Service Code. For Code complaints, the Commission expects the matter to have been raised first within the department, following its internal route, unless there is a good reason, such as a fear of reprisal. The Commission can decline cases that are out of time, that duplicate a case, that concern a matter outside the Code, such as a purely personal grievance, or that are better dealt with by another route, for example an employment tribunal. It does not deal with employment disputes about pay, conditions, or personal treatment, which have their own procedures. The Commission may ask the department for information and can interview people. Its decisions are published in anonymised form where appropriate. If it finds a breach, it can make recommendations to the department, for example about remedial action, and the department is expected to respond. The Commission does not have power to discipline individuals or overturn ministerial decisions, but it reports annually to Parliament and its findings carry weight. The Commission also publishes Recruitment Principles, audits departments' compliance and hears complaints from candidates. The Commissioners are appointed under the rules for public appointments, not by the Prime Minister alone, and are independent of government. This independence supports confidence that civil servants can raise concerns safely and that appointments are on merit.

questions.prompt: A civil servant makes a complaint to the Commission about a pay dispute. What is likely to happen?

options.text: The Commission will rule on the pay but only if the department's process has finished
The Commission will refer it to the Treasury, which sets pay for civil servants
The Commission will accept it, as any unfair treatment of a civil servant is covered
The Commission will decline it, since pay is an employment matter outside the Code

questions.hint: Pay disputes are outside its remit.

questions.prompt: When might the Commission accept a Code complaint without it being raised in the department first?

options.text: If the person dislikes their manager and wants a quicker route
If the matter is minor and can be dealt with easily
If there is a good reason, such as fear of reprisal
If a minister is involved, whatever the circumstances

questions.hint: Good reasons can excuse internal route.

questions.prompt: Which outcome can the Commission produce after finding a breach?

options.text: Recommendations to the department
A dismissal of the official concerned
A fine against the minister who gave the instruction
A court order requiring the department to change its practice

questions.prompt: Which two main functions does the Commission have?

options.text: Setting civil service pay and hearing employment disputes between staff and departments
Regulating recruitment and hearing appeals about breaches of the Civil Service Code
Choosing ministers and auditing the spending of departments
Auditing budgets and drafting legislation for Parliament

questions.prompt: Why is the Commission's independence important?

options.text: It allows the Commission to overrule ministers whenever it disagrees with a policy
It supports confidence that concerns can be raised safely and appointments are on merit
It lets the Commission set the department's recruitment targets each year
It frees the Commission from reporting its findings to anyone outside government

questions.prompt: Which cases might the Commission decline?

options.text: Those from senior officials, which are handled by the Treasury
Those that concern honesty, which is outside the Code
Those out of time or better dealt with by another route
Those that concern impartiality, which is outside the Code

questions.prompt: Can the Commission discipline individual officials it finds at fault?

options.text: It can, for every breach of the Code that it finds
It can, but only for senior officials and only with Treasury approval
It can, but only where the minister has asked it to
It cannot; it makes recommendations and reports, and discipline stays with the department

questions.prompt: A candidate believes a department broke the Recruitment Principles. Where can they take their complaint after the department's process?

options.text: To the Civil Service Commission
To the Treasury
To the Speaker of the House of Commons
To the National Audit Office

items.title: L8: Government communications and propriety
items.source: Government Communication Service, Propriety Guidance; Civil Service Code
items.body: Government communications use public money to inform the public about policies, services and rights. The Government Communication Service sets standards through its Propriety Guidance, which says that communications must be relevant to government responsibilities, objective and explanatory, not biased or polemical, not party political, and must represent value for money. Civil servants working in communications must be politically impartial and must not use public resources to promote a party or criticise opponents. Campaigns should be based on evidence of need, for example public health or recruitment campaigns, and should be evaluated. Press offices handle media enquiries, publish press releases and prepare ministers for interviews, but they do not do party-political rebuttal. Where a minister makes a political point in a speech, a special adviser would normally support that work, while officials support the government business. Social media accounts of government departments are official channels and must follow the same rules. Content must be accurate and not misleading. Use of images and data must comply with copyright and data protection. In an election period, departmental communications are restricted to essential information. Officials should also be cautious about making statements that could affect markets, or about matters before the courts, where comments might prejudice proceedings. Communications may be reviewed by the National Audit Office or the Advertising Standards Authority for some activities. The Government Communication Service also encourages inclusive communications, using plain English, accessible formats and translations where needed. If an official is asked to draft something that is party political, they should decline and raise it with their manager.

questions.prompt: A minister's office asks the press office to draft a press release that criticises the opposition's record. What should the press office do?

options.text: Draft it as asked, because the release supports the minister's work
Decline the party-political element and offer an objective, explanatory release
Draft it but tone down the language so that it reads as less partisan
Draft it in the minister's name only, with no department branding on it

questions.hint: Official communications must not be party political.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a requirement of the Propriety Guidance?

options.text: Communications must support the governing party's policies
Communications must be as short as possible
Communications must avoid all controversial subjects
Communications must be objective and explanatory

questions.prompt: Why might officials be cautious about commenting on a matter before the courts?

options.text: Courts must approve all government statements before they are made
Government is never allowed to talk about courts
Comments could prejudice proceedings
The Speaker forbids comments on legal cases

questions.prompt: A department wants to run a campaign to recruit more staff to a service. What is the principle to follow?

options.text: Base it on evidence of need and evaluate it
Run it only in the weeks before an election
Make it as eye-catching as possible, whatever it costs
Avoid measuring results, since the aim is awareness

questions.prompt: Who normally supports a minister's party-political speeches?

options.text: The press office
The permanent secretary
The special adviser
The Government Communication Service

questions.prompt: A departmental social media post contains an inaccurate statistic. What should happen?

options.text: Leave it in place, because deleting a post draws more attention to the mistake
Correct it promptly, because official channels must be accurate
Defend it, since the figure came from the department's own analysts
Replace it with a different figure without any note that it was changed

questions.prompt: What are departmental communications restricted to during the pre-election period?

options.text: Only ministerial speeches
Only advertising campaigns
Nothing at all
Essential information

questions.prompt: An official is asked to use official social media to promote a party rally. What should they do?

options.text: Decline and raise it with their manager, since official channels cannot promote a party
Do it quickly while the press office is busy with other matters
Do it outside office hours so that official time is not used
Do it if the minister confirms the request in writing

questions.hint: Official resources cannot support party activity.

items.title: L8: Operational delivery: priorities under pressure
items.source: Civil Service Code; Equality Act 2010; departmental service standards
items.body: Operational delivery staff handle large volumes of work in areas such as benefits, tax, passports and borders. When demand rises or staff are short, managers must decide which work to prioritise. The principles are lawfulness, fairness and protection of those at risk. Legal deadlines come first, for example statutory time limits for responding to some requests or processing certain applications. Cases involving vulnerable customers, risk of harm, or urgent need, such as hardship or safeguarding issues, are normally treated as priority. Managers should also consider consistency, so that similar cases are treated similarly, and the Equality Act, so that groups are not disadvantaged by how work is allocated. Decisions about prioritisation should be made with authority, using criteria that are written down and can be explained to customers, ministers and Parliament. Where a backlog builds, the department should be honest with customers about waiting times, give clear information and offer help to people who need it. It should not close cases or alter records to make performance look better. Managing performance data honestly is part of the Code, and targets must not distort behaviour. Staff who feel pressure to cut corners should raise the matter with managers. Quality checking continues even in busy periods, because errors create further work and harm. Transparency with ministers is vital: they should know about backlogs and risks, so they are not surprised and can decide on action. Escalating early allows resources to be moved, overtime authorised, or process changes introduced. Managers should also look after staff wellbeing, because sustained pressure affects quality.

questions.prompt: A backlog is building. Which cases would normally be dealt with first?

options.text: Those that can be closed quickest, which reduces the backlog figure fastest
Those from customers who have complained most often to the department
Those with legal deadlines or involving vulnerability or risk of harm
Those from the largest region, where the most customers live

questions.hint: Legal duties and risk come first.

questions.prompt: A team leader suggests closing old cases without action to improve the backlog figures. What is the problem?

options.text: It would misrepresent performance and harm customers, breaching honesty and integrity
It is acceptable if the cases are old and nobody has chased them recently
It is acceptable if the headline figures improve and ministers are told about the change
It is acceptable if the minister approves the way the backlog is reported

questions.prompt: Why should prioritisation criteria be written down?

options.text: So that managers can avoid responsibility when decisions are challenged
So that decisions are consistent and can be explained
So that staff do not need to use judgement
So that the Treasury can change them at any time

questions.prompt: When a backlog builds, what should the department tell customers?

options.text: Nothing, because explaining delays only produces more calls and complaints
Reassurance that there is no delay, until the backlog is cleared
That the delay arises from customers not supplying enough information
Honest information about likely waiting times and how to get help if the matter is urgent

questions.prompt: Why are ministers told early about backlogs and risks?

options.text: So that they can reassign individual cases to be handled by the private office
So that they can decide which staff are responsible for the backlog
So that they are not surprised and can decide on action such as extra resource
So that the backlog can be presented to Parliament in the best light

questions.prompt: A staff member feels under pressure to skip quality checks. What should they do?

options.text: Skip the checks on the simplest cases only, to meet the weekly target
Carry on, since quality is the manager's responsibility, not theirs
Warn the customers directly that their cases may contain errors
Raise it with their manager, because errors create more work and more harm later

questions.prompt: Which factor must be considered when allocating work to avoid disadvantaging certain groups?

options.text: The Equality Act
The Official Secrets Act
The Public Records Act
The Procurement Act

questions.prompt: A target encourages staff to close calls quickly, but customers with complex needs are being cut off. What does this show?

options.text: That targets are never useful in public services
A target can distort behaviour and harm service
That customers should be redirected to other services
That calls should not be recorded

items.title: L8: Contracts, grants and the delivery model choice
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money, Annex on grants; Government Functional Standard GovS 008 Commercial
items.body: Departments can pay for services in different ways, and the choice affects accountability and risk. A contract is a legally binding agreement in which a supplier provides goods or services in return for payment. It is used when the department is buying something for its own purposes, and it is subject to procurement rules. A grant is money given to a recipient to support activity that serves a wider public purpose, with conditions attached, and the recipient decides how to deliver it within those conditions. Grants are not subject to procurement competition rules in the same way but must follow Treasury and Cabinet Office grant standards, which require clear objectives, fair and open application processes where possible, due diligence, monitoring, and arrangements to recover money if conditions are not met. A department also decides whether to deliver a service itself, to commission it from a supplier, or to use an arm's length body. Delivering in-house gives control but needs capacity. Contracting can bring expertise and flexibility, but the department remains accountable and must manage the contract. Grants give independence to the recipient but less control over delivery. Officials should therefore consider the purpose of the spending: if the department wants a specific service for its own use, a contract fits; if it wants to support an independent organisation's activity, a grant may fit; mislabelling a contract as a grant to avoid competition is improper. Whatever the route, the accounting officer must be satisfied on regularity, propriety, value for money and feasibility. Data protection, fraud risk and conflicts of interest must be managed. Where payment is based on results, the measures must be robust and not open to gaming.

questions.prompt: A department wants a charity to run a local project of the charity's own design that supports a government aim. Which form fits best?

options.text: A contract for services
A grant with conditions
A direct employment arrangement
A loan to the charity

questions.prompt: A department wants a company to build a system for its own use. Which form fits best?

options.text: A contract subject to procurement rules
A grant paid in instalments with conditions
A donation made under the department's charity powers
A secondment of the company's staff to the department

questions.hint: Contracts buy services for the department.

questions.prompt: Calling a contract a grant to avoid competition is what?

options.text: Acceptable if the sum is small and the supplier is well known
Acceptable if the supplier is a charity with a public purpose
Acceptable if the minister has approved the arrangement
Improper, because it avoids rules designed to secure fairness and value for money

questions.prompt: Which feature is typical of good grant management?

options.text: Few conditions, so the recipient has maximum freedom to spend as it sees fit
Monitoring left out after payment, so as not to interfere with the recipient
Clear objectives, due diligence, monitoring and arrangements to recover money if conditions are broken
Payment of the full sum at the start, with checks only if a complaint is made

questions.prompt: What is a drawback of contracting a service out?

options.text: The department hands over accountability, so the supplier answers to Parliament
The department remains accountable and has to manage the contract actively
The service cannot be measured, because the supplier controls the data
Procurement rules no longer apply once a contract has been signed

questions.prompt: What is a genuine advantage of delivering a service in-house?

options.text: It reduces the accountability of the minister for the service
It avoids the need for any staffing capacity or expertise
It removes any data protection or fraud risks
It gives the department greater control over how the service is delivered

questions.prompt: Payment by results is used. What must the measures be?

options.text: As simple as possible, whatever their reliability
Chosen by the supplier
Robust and not open to gaming
Kept secret from the supplier

questions.prompt: Which standard must the accounting officer be satisfied on, whichever route is chosen?

options.text: Regularity, propriety, value for money and feasibility
Popularity, speed, size and visibility to ministers
Branding, price, location and reputation of the supplier
Source of funds, scale of spend, sector and duration
